summary: Describes the X.500 directory information models as used in LDAP, which define how directory entries, attributes and schema are structured. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4512 describes how LDAP represents directory data. It defines the tree of entries, the attributes and classes that describe each entry, and the schema rules that constrain the directory.

questions: what is the ldap information model
what is a distinguished name in ldap
what are structural and auxiliary object classes
subtitle: The LDAP model for directory entries, attributes, names, schema, and server information.

tldr.problem: LDAP clients and servers need shared rules for how directory data is organized, named, constrained, and described.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4512 adapts X.500 information models for LDAP: entries form a tree, attributes hold typed values, object classes constrain entries, and schema and server information can be queried.
tldr.outcome: The document defines the model portion of the LDAP technical specification and replaces specified parts of earlier LDAP RFCs.

today: RFC 4512 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006. Its text obsoletes specified parts of RFC 2251, RFC 2252, and RFC 2256, and all of RFC 3674; the unit metadata lists no later update.

sections.title: Directory Information Models
sections.content:
A directory is a collection of systems that cooperate to provide directory services. Its information is the Directory Information Base (DIB), held in parts by servers and accessed by users through clients.

The DIB contains user information and administrative or operational information. RFC 4512 describes both models, plus the subschema model and the model used to describe a directory server.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory stores information across cooperating servers. Some data describes objects that users look up; other data supports directory operation and administration.

sections.title: Entries, Attributes and the Directory Tree
sections.content:
A directory entry is a named collection of attributes and the basic unit stored in the directory. Entries are organized in a Directory Information Tree (DIT), where each entry has a parent and may have child entries.

An attribute description identifies an attribute type and optional tags; an attribute has one or more values. The type determines the value syntax, whether multiple values are allowed, and how values are compared. Values equivalent under the equality rule cannot both appear in one attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Each directory entry has a place in a tree and contains attributes such as names or other values. Attribute types specify what values are allowed and how they are compared.

sections.title: Relative and Distinguished Names
sections.content:
A Relative Distinguished Name (RDN) identifies an entry among the children of its parent. It contains one or more attribute-value assertions, and each RDN must be unique among sibling entries.

A Distinguished Name (DN) joins the entry's RDN to its parent's DN. The resulting name identifies one entry in the tree. An alias entry provides an alternative name and identifies its target with an aliasedObjectName attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: An RDN distinguishes an entry from its siblings. Joining the RDNs from an entry up through its parents forms the full DN used to identify it.

sections.title: Object Classes and Entry Rules
sections.content:
An object class describes a family of objects and the attributes required or allowed for its entries. Classes may inherit from other classes, and every entry belongs to the abstract class top.

Structural classes describe the entry's real-world object, and each object or alias entry has one structural class chain. Auxiliary classes add allowed attributes and can be added or removed when the schema permits. The structural class cannot be changed.
sections.plainLanguage: An object class defines which attributes an entry must or may contain. Structural classes describe the entry's main type, while auxiliary classes can add permitted attributes.

sections.title: Directory Schema
sections.content:
The schema defines constraints on the directory tree, entry names, attributes, and value matching. It can prevent entries from appearing in invalid positions or holding attributes and values that do not fit their definitions.

Schema definitions identify objects using numeric object identifiers and may include short names, descriptions, inheritance, required and allowed attributes, matching rules, and syntax. LDAP servers can publish schema in subschema entries for clients to inspect.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema is the set of rules that controls which entries and values are valid. Clients can query a server's published schema instead of assuming every server supports the same details.

sections.title: Operational Attributes and the Root DSE
sections.content:
Servers maintain operational attributes for administration, such as creator and modification names and timestamps. These attributes are not normally returned in search results unless a client requests them by name.

The root DSE is the server-specific entry whose DN has zero RDNs. A client can read it to discover information such as naming contexts, supported LDAP versions, controls, extensions, features, and SASL mechanisms. Servers that cache or shadow entries must preserve the originating server's access controls.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers keep operational information that is separate from user-provided attributes. A client can read the root DSE to learn what the server supports and which parts of the directory it serves.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Servers must recognize the names of schema elements defined by the specification and ensure entries conform to schema rules. Some features, including alias entries and certain DIT rules, are optional. Clients should read the subschema rather than assume that every server supports the same elements.

Directory attributes may describe people, organizations, or devices, and may be sensitive. The RFC points to LDAP authentication and security specifications for access protection and updates the LDAP descriptors registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients should discover a server's schema before relying on optional features. Directory operators must also protect attributes that contain sensitive information.
